title: The Evening Brief: Rybakina Locks No. 1, Sets Up Sabalenka Final
dek: Rybakina beat Gauff to clinch the world No. 1 ranking and a Saturday final against Sabalenka, while NFL openers left a trail of injuries and the Clippers investigation moved into federal territory.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Rybakina's semifinal win over Gauff secures the No. 1 ranking and sets a Sabalenka-Rybakina final Saturday, while the day's other stories center on injuries, discipline, and an escalating federal probe rather than settled outcomes.
bottom_line: Rybakina's win over Gauff clinched the world No. 1 ranking and set up a Saturday final against Sabalenka, the first top-two-seed US Open final since 2013, giving tennis a clean resolution while most of Friday's other stories left matters open. NFL openers produced a cluster of injuries, Brown's high-ankle sprain, Darnold's hip, Tagovailoa's oblique, without settling who plays where next. The Clippers matter moved from league penalties into a federal criminal investigation still in its earliest stages, and the SEC-LSU dispute paused short of expulsion but left sanctions and a federal lawsuit unresolved. The honest read is that Friday clarified one championship matchup while leaving several personnel and legal questions genuinely open. Saturday's final, Sunday's Week 1 games, and the rescheduled SEC-LSU hearing are the next checkpoints.
body: The US Open women's draw resolved its biggest open question Friday: Elena Rybakina defeated Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 in the semifinal, a result that guarantees Rybakina the world No. 1 ranking when rankings update Monday, September 14, ending Aryna Sabalenka's 99-week reign at the top. Sabalenka defeated Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2 in the other semifinal, meaning the final Saturday will pit the tournament's top two seeds against each other for the first time at the US Open since 2013, when Serena Williams beat Victoria Azarenka. As reported this morning, all four top seeds, Sabalenka, Rybakina, Pegula and Gauff, had reached the semifinals for the first time since 1975, a convergence that has now narrowed to its final two.

Elsewhere, the day's throughline was injury and disruption rather than resolution. The Seahawks beat the Patriots 13-10 in Wednesday's season opener, with Drake Maye throwing three interceptions in the fourth quarter, including the game-deciding pick with 26 seconds left that NBC's Cris Collinsworth called indefensible from field-goal range. New England compounded that loss by placing wide receiver A.J. Brown on injured reserve with a high-ankle sprain suffered in the same game, sidelining him at least four weeks through games against Pittsburgh, Jacksonville, Buffalo, Las Vegas and the Jets. Seattle has its own uncertainty: quarterback Sam Darnold left the same game with a hip injury, a fracture ruled out but further testing pending and no timeline given for Week 2. In Atlanta, Tua Tagovailoa is day-to-day with an oblique strain from Thursday practice, his availability for Sunday's opener against Pittsburgh unclear, with Cooper Rush or undrafted rookie Jack Strand as the fallback options.

The Dodgers' stretch run carries its own mix of promise and caution. Josue De Paula, the club's No. 6-ranked prospect on MLB Pipeline's Top 100, is set to debut Friday in Miami after skipping Triple-A entirely, the first Dodgers position player to do so under Andrew Friedman. That call-up comes as Shohei Ohtani sits on the 15-day injured list for left knee soreness and a right biceps injury, eligible to return September 23 with five regular-season games left before the postseason. The MLB playoff picture itself remains unsettled entering the weekend, with the Rays leading the AL East by 3 games, the Phillies leading the first NL Wild Card by 1 game over the Cubs, and the Padres up 0.5 games over the Diamondbacks for the final Wild Card spot.

Off the field, two stories moved from threat toward uneasy pause without resolving. LSU removed former NFL players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris from its roster after the SEC filed an amended lawsuit that set the stage for possible expulsion; the SEC's Thursday presidents' videoconference produced no penalty announcement, only a statement that discussions would continue, and the federal lawsuit remains active with its hearing postponed. The Clippers investigation escalated further: the U.S. attorney's office in Brooklyn has opened a criminal investigation into the team, owner Steve Ballmer, and Kawhi Leonard over alleged salary-cap circumvention, following an NBA probe that found rule violations. At least one subpoena has been issued, with the case described as in its earliest stages. Separately, former NFL running back LeShon Johnson was sentenced to five years in federal prison for operating a large-scale dogfighting ring, having surrendered 190 dogs, the largest number seized from one individual in a federal dogfighting case according to the Department of Justice. And the NFL's international push reached a new marker Friday, as the 49ers beat the Rams in the first-ever NFL regular-season game in Australia, drawing a sellout crowd of 100,021 at the MCG in Melbourne as part of a four-year deal between the league and the city.

The reporting does not offer a single driver tying these threads together beyond timing: openers, debuts and semifinals landing in the same 48 hours produced both clarity, in tennis, and unresolved situations everywhere else, from injury statuses to legal proceedings.

What to watch: Saturday's US Open final between Rybakina and Sabalenka, the first top-two-seed final there since 2013. Sunday's Week 1 NFL slate, including whether Tagovailoa plays for Atlanta and how New England's offense functions without Brown. Seattle's forthcoming update on Darnold's hip. De Paula's early major-league at-bats in Miami. The rescheduled temporary restraining order hearing in the SEC-LSU federal case, and any further filings in the Clippers investigation as it moves past its earliest stages.
